title: Three perfect days in Miami: Calle Ocho, the Book Fair and a Berlin collection
dek: The Miami Book Fair's Street Fair takes over downtown (free on Friday), PAMM hangs nearly 100 modern masterpieces from Berlin, and the Heat host Oklahoma City on Sunday night.

hero.caption: The Freedom Tower on Biscayne Boulevard, a few blocks from the Miami Book Fair's downtown Street Fair.

intro:
The weekend before Thanksgiving is a good one to have Miami mostly to yourself. The air has cooled, the art-week crowds of early December have not arrived, and the city is spending its weekend on the mainland, downtown and in the old neighborhoods west and south of it.

The reason is the **Miami Book Fair**, which opened its 43rd edition on November 15 and finishes with its three-day **Street Fair** from Friday to Sunday: booksellers, food and music spread through the blocks around Miami Dade College's Wolfson Campus. Friday is free for everyone; Saturday and Sunday need a ticket.

Across Biscayne Boulevard, the Pérez Art Museum Miami has just opened *Picasso–Klee–Matisse: Masterpieces from the Museum Berggruen*, nearly 100 modern works on loan from Berlin and the museum's first show devoted entirely to modern art. Kaseya Center hosts John Summit on Friday and Saturday nights and the Heat on Sunday evening, and the Hurricanes play Virginia Tech at Hard Rock Stadium on Saturday.

The plan follows that calendar and stays mostly off the beach. Friday starts with cafecito on Calle Ocho in Little Havana, crosses to the free day of the Street Fair, and ends back on Calle Ocho with daiquiris and live music. Saturday is Coconut Grove and the gardens: Vizcaya in the morning, a Cuban diner for lunch, the palms and orchids at Fairchild, and dinner at Ariete. Sunday is Wynwood's bakery and murals, a French lunch, the Berggruen pictures at PAMM and the Heat.

days.title: Friday: Calle Ocho and the Street Fair
days.intro: Little Havana at both ends of the day, and the free first day of the Book Fair's Street Fair downtown in between.

stops.name: Versailles
stops.text: Miami's best-known Cuban restaurant, all mirrors and chandeliers, and still the place where the city's arguments about Cuba tend to start. Begin at the ventanita, the walk-up window on the side, with a colada (strong, sweet espresso meant to be poured into tiny cups and shared) and a pastelito, then go inside if you want a proper breakfast. It opens at 8 a.m. every day, so there is no need to rush, and the walk-up window is quicker than waiting for a table.

stops.name: Calle Ocho and Domino Park
stops.text: Drive or ride about two miles east to SW 15th Avenue and walk the stretch of Calle Ocho between 12th and 17th avenues. At Máximo Gómez Park, known to everyone as Domino Park, members of the domino club play daily and do not much like being hurried. The star plaques on the Calle Ocho Walk of Fame honor Celia Cruz and Gloria Estefan, among others, and the Tower Theater at 1508 SW 8th St. is a 1926 cinema remodeled in Art Deco in 1931. Detour one block to Cuban Memorial Boulevard on SW 13th Avenue for the Brigade 2506 torch.

stops.name: El Rey de las Fritas
stops.text: The frita is Miami's own burger: a seasoned beef-and-pork patty on a Cuban roll, piled with a nest of thin, crisp potato sticks. This inexpensive, quick diner on Calle Ocho makes one of the best, and the souped-up versions are worth the extra napkins. It is the right weight for an afternoon on your feet. Expect a counter-and-booth room, fast service and a line at peak lunch hour; it moves.

stops.name: Miami Book Fair: the Street Fair
stops.text: The final three days of the Book Fair turn the blocks around Miami Dade College's Wolfson Campus into a street fair of booksellers, publishers, food and music, and Friday, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., is free for everyone. Browse the stalls, check the author schedule on the fair's site for readings, and buy the book you did not know you wanted. Gates open at 9 a.m. The college garage at 500 NE Second Ave. is the closest parking, but the free Metromover is easier.

stops.name: Night Market at Miami Worldcenter
stops.text: Every Friday from 5 to 9 p.m., vendors set up along the Paseo at Miami Worldcenter, next to the old Pan Am globe at 850 NE 2nd Ave., a short walk from the Book Fair. Vendors change from week to week, so treat it as a browse and a snack rather than a meal. It is a good way to see the newest part of downtown and fills the gap before dinner. Then take a taxi back west to Calle Ocho, about 15 minutes.

stops.name: Café La Trova
stops.text: Julio Cabrera, a classically trained Cuban cantinero inducted into Bartender Magazine's Hall of Fame, runs the bar here with chef Michelle Bernstein in the kitchen. Order a daiquiri or a mojito, made the old Havana way, and the arroz con pollo. Musicians play nightly behind the bar and on the small stage, and by nine the room is dancing. The bar is ranked among North America's best, so book ahead for a Friday table.

stops.name: Ball & Chain
stops.text: One of Little Havana's longstanding nightlife venues, a few blocks west on Calle Ocho, with live Latin music through the week. Check the events page for Friday's lineup; many nights have no cover with an RSVP. If you have never danced salsa, this is a forgiving place to try, and the crowd mixes regulars of every age with people who came in off the street.

days.title: Saturday: Coconut Grove and the gardens
days.intro: Bay-front Italianate grandeur in the morning, a tropical garden in the afternoon and Miami's most personal Michelin dinner.

stops.name: Ophelia
stops.text: A bakery run out of a trailer, open only Wednesday to Saturday, which is why you are here on a Saturday at 8:30. Order the breakfast sandwich and a coffee cinnamon roll, and buy a slice of olive oil cake for later. Lines build after 8 a.m., so come early. It is a few minutes' drive from Vizcaya, the morning's next stop.

stops.name: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
stops.text: James Deering's winter house on Biscayne Bay, finished in the 1910s, is the grandest room in Miami: a Mediterranean-style villa full of European antiques, with formal gardens running down to a stone barge in the bay. Do the house first, then the gardens before the midday sun. It opens at 9:30 a.m. every day except Tuesday and closes at 4:30 p.m. Guided behind-the-scenes tours cost $24 to $39 and include admission.

stops.name: Chug's Diner
stops.text: A Cuban diner in the middle of the Grove's village, with booths and counter seats. Order the Cuban completa or the frita patty melt if you skipped one yesterday, and leave room for pie. It is a five-minute walk from Ariete, so you will pass tonight's dinner on the way, and from Peacock Park and the bay if you want to walk lunch off.

stops.name: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden
stops.text: About 20 minutes south along Old Cutler Road, 83 acres of palms, cycads, orchids and lakes. Take the free narrated tram tour to get your bearings, then walk to Wings of the Tropics, the butterfly and hummingbird house. It is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; weekend adult tickets are $27.95 online, $5 less than at the gate, and parking is free. The holiday NightGarden light show also runs on select nights this season, if you want to come back after dark.

stops.name: Ariete
stops.text: Michael Beltran opened Ariete in 2016 and has held a Michelin star since 2022, cooking food that sounds like Miami: croquetas, braised oxtail and a Cuban sandwich turned into a pithivier. The dish to plan around is the canard à la presse, a duck pressed at the table into its own sauce; there is also a tasting menu. This is a special-occasion room, so reserve, and allow two hours.

days.title: Sunday: Wynwood, Museum Park and the Heat
days.intro: Bread and murals in Wynwood, then the Berlin pictures at PAMM and an early tip-off on the bay.

stops.name: Zak the Baker
stops.text: Zak Stern's kosher bakery has been the neighborhood's bread since 2012, and its café is open Sunday to Friday from 7 a.m. Order the babka, a bagel or an egg sandwich, and take a loaf of the naturally leavened bread home if you have a kitchen. Sit inside or grab from the counter; it is a two-block walk to the Wynwood Walls, which open at 10:30.

stops.name: Wynwood Walls
stops.text: The outdoor street-art museum that has anchored Wynwood since 2009, with murals by well over 100 artists from around the world, repainted in part every year. Go at opening, 10:30 a.m., before the light is flat and the paths are crowded, then walk the streets around it, where the murals are free. Doors close 30 minutes before the 6:30 p.m. closing; buy tickets online.

stops.name: Pastis
stops.text: The Miami branch of Keith McNally's New York brasserie, with a patio and a dining room that feel like a Paris side street. At brunch order croissants and pain au chocolat for the table, then onion soup, steak tartare or a niçoise; at the bar, the cheeseburger and steak frites have their own following. It suits a group, and it is a short ride from Museum Park. Reserve on Resy for Sunday.

stops.name: Pérez Art Museum Miami
stops.text: *Picasso–Klee–Matisse* fills PAMM's largest galleries with nearly 100 works from Berlin's Museum Berggruen: Picasso's 1904 portrait of Jaume Sabartés, Klee's *Landscape in Blue*, a Matisse cut-out and Giacometti's thin figures, hung beside Rivera, Torres-García and Lam from PAMM's own collection. Then see *Basquiat: Figures, Signs, Symbols* and step onto the bay-front terraces under the hanging gardens. Open 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sunday.

stops.name: La Cañita
stops.text: Michelle Bernstein's Cuban-Caribbean restaurant at Bayside Marketplace looks out on the marina and is a five-minute walk from the arena, which makes it the right early dinner on a game night. Order the conch fritters, the jerk wings and the arroz con pollo or whole fried snapper, with a piña colada. Leave by 5:45 for tip-off; there is no need to drive between the two.

stops.name: Heat vs. Thunder at Kaseya Center
stops.text: The Heat host Oklahoma City at 6 p.m., an early Sunday tip that gets you out by about 8:30. The arena sits on Biscayne Bay at 601 Biscayne Blvd., a short walk from PAMM and Bayside, with the free Metromover stopping outside. Buy through the team or the NBA's official resale. After the game, the Metromover runs back toward Brickell and the downtown hotels.

stay.name: Mr. C Miami Coconut Grove
stay.text: The Cipriani family's Miami hotel, opened in 2019, designed by Arquitectonica with interiors by Martin Brudnizki. Every room has a private balcony, the hotel looks out over Biscayne Bay, and the top floor holds a rooftop pool and Bellini, the Italian restaurant and bar where you can order the drink the family made famous at Harry's Bar in Venice. It puts you minutes from Vizcaya, Chug's and Ariete for Saturday.

stay.name: The Biltmore Hotel
stay.text: George Merrick's 1926 landmark, celebrating its centennial this year, with its tower over Coral Gables and one of the largest hotel pools in the continental United States, about 600,000 gallons. It is the old-Miami choice: a short drive to Calle Ocho on Friday and to Fairchild and the Grove on Saturday, and quiet at night.

stay.name: citizenM Miami Worldcenter
stay.text: A compact, well-designed hotel at 700 NE 2nd Ave., with a rooftop pool and bar looking over downtown and a lobby bar that serves food around the clock. It is a block from the Friday Night Market, a few minutes' walk from the Book Fair and Kaseya Center, and on the Metromover line, so you can skip a car for two of the three days.

events.name: Miami Book Fair: Street Fair
events.when: Fri. and Sat. 10 a.m.–7 p.m., Sun. 10 a.m.–6 p.m.
events.where: Downtown, around Miami Dade College's Wolfson Campus
events.text: The closing three days of the 43rd Book Fair. Free for everyone on Friday; Saturday and Sunday tickets are $12 for adults, $18 for a multi-day pass, and children 12 and under are free.

events.name: Night Market at Miami Worldcenter
events.where: The Paseo at Miami Worldcenter, 850 NE 2nd Ave.
events.text: The weekly Friday market beside the Pan Am globe, a short walk from the Book Fair.

events.name: John Summit: CTRL Escape Tour
events.when: Fri. and Sat., doors 7 p.m., show 8 p.m.
events.text: Two nights of the house DJ's arena tour. All ages, 18 and over recommended; expect busy streets around the arena both nights.

events.name: Miami Hurricanes vs. Virginia Tech
events.text: The Canes' ACC home game, moved from Friday to Saturday. Hard Rock Stadium is about 30 minutes north of downtown.

events.name: Indigo Hands: family storytime and dyeing workshop
events.text: Author Sita Singh reads, then families try indigo dyeing by hand.

events.name: Miami Heat vs. Oklahoma City Thunder
events.text: The Heat's only home game of the weekend, an early Sunday tip-off.

know: From Miami International (MIA), the free MIA Mover runs to the Miami Intermodal Center, where Metrorail goes downtown in about 25 to 30 minutes. A taxi or ride-hail downtown is usually 20 to 30 minutes. Fort Lauderdale (FLL) is the other airport, farther north.

The downtown Metromover is free and loops past the Book Fair, Miami Worldcenter, Bayside, Kaseya Center and PAMM. Metrorail and Metrobus fares are $2.25 a ride. Little Havana, Coconut Grove and Fairchild are easiest by car or ride-hail.

Downtown is crowded all weekend: the Street Fair runs Friday to Sunday, John Summit plays Kaseya Center on Friday and Saturday nights, and the Heat play there at 6 p.m. Sunday. Use the Metromover instead of looking for parking near Biscayne Boulevard.
On Saturday the Hurricanes play Virginia Tech at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens; allow extra time on the roads north of the city, including routes to Fort Lauderdale airport.
Museum days: PAMM is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays and open 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Friday to Sunday; Vizcaya is closed on Tuesdays; Zak the Baker is closed on Saturdays and Ophelia on Sundays.
Thanksgiving is Thursday, November 26, so airports and highways will be busier from the following Tuesday. If you are staying on, book holiday-week restaurants now.
Sunset is around 5:30 p.m., so plan garden and mural time for the morning and early afternoon.
Many Miami restaurants add a service charge to the bill, so check before tipping. Where none is added, 18 to 20 percent is usual.
